blocks.text: Cleopatra, wise, most beautiful, and far surpassing all other women, had for the care of her hair and nails Charmiuno and Taïra. But what do these names signify? See now Tzetzes, at once a Syrian and an Ishmaelite, explaining them to you in their languages. In the language of the Hebrews as well as of the Syrians, Charmi signifies the vine, and Uno the dove, which the Greeks call the oenas dove. But among the Ishmaelites, I mean those descended from Hagar, understand that Taïra signifies [II, 526] the dove to me. From this gather that in Plutarch for Εἴρας [Eiras], and in Galen for Νάειρα [Naeira], one must write Τάειρας [Taeiras] or Τάειρα [Taeira], as in Tzetzes, who indeed writes this word correctly but interprets it wrongly. For the Arabic طاير [ṭāyir] taïr, or طايرة [ṭāyira] taira, does not signify a dove, but a bird in general. Hence for the Chaldeans טייר tajer means to take auguries. Nor should Charmiuno have been divided into Charmi and Uno, but into כרם charm and יונא juno. Meanwhile there is no doubt that Charmiuno, or Charmiona, is truly οἰνάς [oinas]. So יונה jona by itself is not οἰνὰς [oinas], but any dove. This being granted, no reason appears why יונה jona should be named from wine. Therefore something else must be sought. Nor perhaps will it be absurd to think that doves were called by their native name יונים jonim, as if Greek ones. For the Greeks were formerly called Ἴωνες [Iōnes] Iones, as we have proved elsewhere; and in Hebrew יונים jonim, with the same letters, although today they pronounce javanim, because that pleased the Masoretes. Two things chiefly suggest that doves were named from this. One, that in Pliny, book 10, chapter 29, Theophrastus reports that doves were imported into Asia. The other, that mythical history amply shows that there were doves in Greece from all time. Thus 1. they say that the Dodonaean dove ^{c)} ἱζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν, αὐδάξασθαι φωνῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ, ὡς χρεὼν εἴη, μαντήϊον αὐτόθι Διὸς γένεσθαι [hizomenēn epi phēgon, audaxasthai phōnē anthrōpinē, hōs chreōn eiē, mantēion autothi Dios genesthai], sitting on a beech tree, said with a human voice that it was fated that an oracle of Jupiter should be founded in that place, which was by far the most ancient of all Greece. 2. As from Noah, so from Deucalion they relate ^{d)} περιστερὰν, ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην, δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ, ἀποπτᾶσαν [peristeran, ek tēs larnakos aphiemenēn, dēlōma genesthai, cheimōnos men eisō palin endyomenēn, eudias de, apoptasan], that a dove, sent out from the ark, was a sign of storm when it returned there, and of fair weather when it flew away. 3. Doves are said to have fed Jupiter, crying as an infant in Crete, with ambrosia brought from Ocean, according to Moero of Byzantium in Athenaeus, book 11,

Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἀρ᾽ ἐνὶ Κρήτῃ τρέφετο μέγας, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τίς νιν Ἠήδει μακάρων. ὁ δ᾽ ἀέξετο πᾶσι μέλεσσι Τὸν μὲν ἄρα τρήρωνες ὑπὸ ζαθέῳ τρέφον ἄντρῳ, Ἀμβροσίην φορέουσαι ἀπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων. [Zeus d᾽ ar᾽ eni Krētē trepheto megas, oud᾽ ara tis nin ēēdei makarōn. ho d᾽ aexeto pasi melessi; ton men ara trērōnes hypo zatheō trephon antrō, ambrosiēn phoreousai ap᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn.]

In Crete great Jupiter was nourished, and none of the Blessed knew him. And he grew in all his limbs. Doves, moreover, fed him in the divine cave, bringing ambrosia from the streams of Ocean. This is taken from Odyssey μ´ [12], where doves

— — ἀμβροσίην Διῒ πατρὶ φέρουσιν [ambrosiēn Dii patri pherousin], — — bring ambrosia to father Jupiter. [II, 527] Hence it is that in Plutarch's Symposium Cleodemus says to the poet Chersias: Εἰ τὴν [col. 4] ἀμβροσίαν τῷ Διῒ πελειάδες τινὲς κομίζουσιν, ὡς ὑμεῖς λέγετε [Ei tēn ambrosian tō Dii peleiades tines komizousin, hōs hymeis legete], If certain doves bring ambrosia to Jupiter, as you poets say. 4. At Aegium, a city of Achaea, Jupiter, changed into a dove, is said to have lain with the maiden Phthia. Athenaeus, book 9: Αὐτοκράτης ἐν τοῖς Ἀχαικοῖς καὶ τὸν Διὰ ἱστορεῖ μεταβαλεῖν τὴν μορφὴν εἰς περιστερὰν, ἐρασθέντα παρθένου Φθίας ὄνομα ἐν Αἰγείῳ [Autokratēs en tois Achaikois kai ton Dia historei metabalein tēn morphēn eis peristeran, erasthenta parthenou Phthias onoma en Aigeiō]. Autocrates in his Achaica relates that Jupiter himself, loving a maiden named Phthia in Aegium, changed his form into a dove. So too Aelian, Varia book 1, chapter 15. 5. The Argonauts, about to pass between the clashing Symplegades, were advised by the seer Phineus to send out a dove, and if it passed through them safely, they too should follow; and this they did. This dove is mentioned by Apollonius, book 2 of the Argonautica, Asclepiades, book 2 of the Τραγῳδούμενα [Tragōdoumena], Apollodorus, book 1 of the Bibliotheca, Hyginus, Fable 19, and not a few others. 6. When Ctesylla, daughter of Alcidamas of Ceos, who died in childbirth, was being carried out for burial, ἐκ τῆς στρομνῆς πελειὰς ἐξέπτη, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς Κτησύλλης ἀφανὲς ἐγένετο [ek tēs stromnēs peleias exeptē, kai to sōma tēs Ktēsyllēs aphanes egeneto], a dove flew out of the bier, and the body of Ctesylla vanished. So Nicander, book 3 of the Ἑτεροιούμενα [Heteroioumena]. Hence Ovid, of Medea borne through the air, Metamorphoses book 7, Fable 12,
